Where AI adoption remains low

Barriers to adoption vary but concerns around cost and output quality remain the top reasons for creatives hesitant to use AI in their work.

Barriers to AI adoption

Barriers to AI adoption

Barriers & concerns by experience level

Reasons for slow adoption

Output quality and reliability

“I believe excessive usage depletes human creativity so I do not rely on AI too much to do all the hammering for me. Also when using it to explore new tools the AI quite often hallucinates about the tools' features or functions and specifications and draws away from the main objective of the project for which the AI is assisting on using the tool which could be some relatively new or unknown tool. This barrier often constricts the reliability of AI to make best possible use of tools such as say Wonder since it guesses about the tools features and visibility rather than realistic introspection. So AI hallucination is a big barrier.”

”

Cost and tool overload

“Subscriptions are a big thing. One subscription costs like $20 for basic tiers and if you don't have at least one it feels like you fall behind. The output isn't the best for big designs so I only really use it for mood boarding or questions. For actual coding, I prompt Claude code or Cursor and then make alterations myself.”

“Too many AI tools to evaluate, frequent model changes, inconsistent outputs between models, and keeping up with rapid updates.”

”

Workflow integration

“AI tools are too scattered right now and there aren't enough ways to harness the actual power of AI. Some tools work awesome but some still require a lot of prompting and iteration. I get into a loop of iterations over iterations that lead to nothing.”

“My main barrier is workflow reliability: keeping context, preserving reasoning, integrating with my existing tools, and reducing cleanup after AI generation.”

”

Privacy and intellectual property

“AI lacks cultural nuances of regional music, vehicle logistics precision, and cinematic standards. Ethically, I am deeply concerned about environmental impacts and severe data privacy risks regarding the potential leak or unauthorized training of my studio's unreleased intellectual property.”

”

Client trust

“Trust: knowing when AI output is reliable enough to use and how to keep the final work from becoming generic. The tools are powerful, but the workflow still requires a lot of human review, taste, and context.”

“I won't say clients don't want AI used but there certainly is a stigma attached. They often want it to not look like AI was used.”

”

Learning and rapid change

“Mostly it's cost prices or AI not producing a good enough result, however, in the past year I have noticed that the quality of things has increased tremendously, so right now my issue is that I am not even aware of all the tools out there and all their capabilities, as it's so many of them! It's hard to keep up at this point.”

”

Loss of craft or judgment

“I worry about reducing my own skills and knowledge by relying too much on AI.”

”

Three distinct phases where AI fuels creative workflows.

Ideation, mockup and refinement. Here’s where AI enters and what creatives protect, mapped against the Human Creativity Benchmark.

Creative workflow breakdown

Inspired by the Human Creativity Benchmark

Creative workflow breakdown

Inspired by the Human Creativity Benchmark

Research & exploration

AI helps me move faster and explore more ideas, but the final design decisions, refinement, and execution come from me as the designer.

Concept development

I share the filled out questionnaire from my client and start by asking AI to help me list out direct and adjacent competitors. Then I ask it to help me conduct research on those brands and the overall industry...

Competitive research

Overall, the AI worked as a creative interlocutor: a tool for contrasting ideas, exploring options, and resolving technical doubts.

Strategy validation

I used Claude and ChatGPT less for drafting and more as a strategic critique tool, pressure-testing positioning, poking holes in messaging, and checking if a brand story actually held up before I finalized it.

Creative review

After completing the designs, I also used AI as a second set of eyes to check whether the ads aligned with the original brief before delivering them to the client.

Conclusions

Conclusions

Conclusions

Conclusions

Three years ago, the story was that AI would replace creatives. That’s not what’s happening.

We surveyed 150k+ creative professionals, and combined this with real marketplace data from Contra. AI adoption is up to over 70% and creatives are earning in entirely new categories. It’s an incredible time for creativity.
